run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_218 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Two questions, two answers. (1) The configured MySQL database testdb contains exactly two tables, holmes_eval_218 and orders (e279a6e6-b1d3-483a-b0f7-9b3e5be18c91-t0). The single row of holmes_eval_218 (id=1, category 'eval_test') carries verification_code = HOLMES-MYSQL-EVAL-218-m4x9k2 (1037c03c-4075-4039-af39-9ade3d15ca8a-t0). (2) The slowness of SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 is a structural problem of the orders table in schema testdb: the table has only the PRIMARY key on id and no index on customer_id (67cfabb7-e695-4b73-8503-01d3aa276232-t1, 495d499e-9c7b-43ed-ac2d-d162ca8c492e-t2), so the optimizer has no possible key and reads the whole table (type=ALL, key=NULL, rows=1000, 'Using where'; 495d499e-9c7b-43ed-ac2d-d162ca8c492e-t0). EXPLAIN ANALYZE confirms a Table scan on orders reading 1000 rows to return 0 (b645fae8-04cf-4122-9834-9773ecbb8894-t0). Important counter-evidence: at the sampled moment the query is not actually slow — the scan costs 0.377 ms on a 1000-row/81,920-byte InnoDB table, and my probe of the same predicate examined 1000 rows in 0.541 ms (b645fae8-04cf-4122-9834-9773ecbb8894-t0, 2286b996-d998-413c-82cc-7ebd7947f7cc-t0). So the missing index is a real, evidence-backed latent cause that scales linearly with table growth, but no slow execution of this statement was observed on this target: slow_query_log is OFF and the server/schema was only created at 2026-11-21T03:40:13, so performance_schema holds no application history of the statement (d02b0ad1-d383-431a-bb56-066103ab1429-t0, d02b0ad1-d383-431a-bb56-066103ab1429-t1, 2286b996-d998-413c-82cc-7ebd7947f7cc-t0). Also note customer_id values only span 2..998, so literal 12345 matches zero rows today (b645fae8-04cf-4122-9834-9773ecbb8894-t1, 495d499e-9c7b-43ed-ac2d-d162ca8c492e-t1); the fix is an index on customer_id, and the recommendation is to enable the slow query log to capture the real slow statements.

claims.text: The database testdb contains exactly two tables: holmes_eval_218 and orders (both schema testdb, type table).
holmes_eval_218 has columns id (int, PK), category varchar(50), verification_code varchar(100), created_at timestamp; its only index is PRIMARY on id.
The one row of holmes_eval_218 (id=1, category 'eval_test', created_at 2026-11-21T03:40:13) has verification_code = HOLMES-MYSQL-EVAL-218-m4x9k2.
orders has columns id (int, PK), customer_id (int NOT NULL), order_date (date NOT NULL), total_amount decimal(10,2), status varchar(20), and its only index is PRIMARY (BTREE, unique) on id.

EXPLAIN of SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 returns select_type SIMPLE, type ALL, possible_keys NULL, key NULL, rows 1000, filtered 10.0, Extra 'Using where' — a full table scan with no usable index for the customer_id predicate; the absence of an index on orders.customer_id is what forces this scan.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the same statement shows 'Table scan on orders (cost=101 rows=1000) (actual time=0.0512..0.377 rows=1000)' feeding 'Filter: (orders.customer_id = 12345) (actual time=0.423..0.423 rows=0)': the whole table is read to produce zero rows, in 0.377 ms at the current data volume.
orders holds 1000 rows across 641 distinct customer_id values, with customer_id ranging 2..998 and order_date 2025-11-22..2026-11-20, so the literal predicate customer_id = 12345 matches 0 rows.

orders is InnoDB, 1000 rows, Data_length 81,920 bytes, Index_length 0, created 2026-11-21T03:40:13; the server is MySQL 8.0.40 with innodb_buffer_pool_size 134,217,728 bytes, so the table fits easily in the buffer pool.
slow_query_log is OFF with long_query_time 10.000000 s, so this server currently records no slow-query log entries at all.

In performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest, the only digests matching orders/customer_id are the probes issued in this investigation: 'EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?' (0.812 ms) and 'EXPLAIN ANALYZE ...' (3.214 ms, avg_rows_examined 1000) and the COUNT probe (0.541 ms, avg_rows_examined 1000); no application execution of 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?' is recorded (performance_schema is enabled, FIRST_SEEN timestamps are 2026-11-21T03:40).

The premise 'slow queries' is not reproduced on this target: the same predicate executes as a 1000-row full scan in 0.377 ms (EXPLAIN ANALYZE actual time) and my equivalent probe in 0.541 ms, and the whole 81,920-byte InnoDB table is far smaller than the 128 MiB buffer pool, so there is no observed latency, IO or sizing evidence of current slowness.

Value skew / parameter sniffing is not the explanation here: the optimizer already estimates filtered 10.0 and still chooses a scan, so the plan does not depend on which customer_id value is supplied (possible_keys is NULL because no index on customer_id exists).

As the orders table grows beyond the current 1000 rows, the cost of this statement grows linearly with table size because every execution reads all rows (avg_rows_examined 1000 per execution) and returns only the handful belonging to one customer; this is the most likely mechanism for slowness at production volume, but it was not observed as actual slow latency in the sampled data.

SELECT * widens each matching row to all five columns (avg_row_length 81 bytes) and prevents an index-only path, so it adds avoidable work once customer_id becomes selective; this is a secondary factor, not the reason for the scan.

Add an index on the predicate column, e.g. CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id), then re-run EXPLAIN to confirm key usage replaces the type=ALL full scan; if the access pattern filters or sorts by date too, a composite (customer_id, order_date) index is the natural choice.
Replace SELECT * with the columns actually needed, and for an order-history read add a deterministic ORDER BY (e.g. order_date DESC, id DESC) with a LIMIT so the index can serve ordering and paging.

To get evidence of actual slow queries, enable slow_query_log (currently OFF; long_query_time is 10 s) or lower long_query_time, and inspect performance_schema digest statistics over a representative window; today the server holds only the few seconds of history created at 2026-11-21T03:40:13.

gaps: No slow execution of 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?' was observed: slow_query_log is OFF and performance_schema history on this server starts at 2026-11-21T03:40:13, so the reported slowness cannot be confirmed or timed on this target.

The statement the application actually runs was never seen executing; only EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE probes of the same predicate were recorded in performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest.
customer_id = 12345 matches no row (customer_id values span only 2..998), so no measurement was possible for a lookup that returns real matching rows.

No application- or connection-pool-side latency for this query was examined (no Prometheus or Jaeger query was made for a DB statement metric for this question), so end-to-end query latency is unknown.

Whether any index changes or configuration changes were made earlier could not be checked: the change_history integration is not available in this Run, and the schema itself was created at 2026-11-21T03:40:13.
next_steps: Have the application owner run the exact production statement via EXPLAIN (and time it) against a production-sized copy of orders, then create index idx_orders_customer_id (or (customer_id, order_date)) and compare plans and timings.
Enable slow_query_log with a threshold below the observed user-facing latency target and capture the real statement digests before changing indexes.
If end-to-end latency matters, correlate the query with application telemetry (traces/metrics) around the reported slow period, since this database target contains only tens of seconds of history.
